$comment: Teaching content for cl_orchestration. The workflow-versus-agent distinction is the most heavily tested idea in Section 3.

knowledgePoints.name: One question separates them
knowledgePoints.teach:
Workflow — a predefined series of Claude calls solving a known problem. You can picture the exact steps ahead of time.

Agent — Claude gets a goal and a set of tools and figures out its own path. Used when you don't know what task or parameters will come in.

Can you picture the steps in advance? Yes → workflow. No → agent.

Everything else follows from that. A workflow's steps are known, so they can be tested individually, optimised individually, and reasoned about when they fail. An agent's cannot, because they do not exist until it runs.

questions.q: Your team is scoping a new automation: extracting structured line items from vendor invoices, where the invoice format, field names, and number of pages are known in advance and identical every time. A teammate argues this should be built as an agent with a broad toolset so it can 'figure things out.' Which single question would settle whether a workflow or an agent is the right design here?
options: Whether the exact steps required to complete the task can be pictured in advance.
Whether the task can be completed using more than one Claude call in sequence.
Whether the workflow needs access to any external tools during execution.
Whether the final output must be returned in a structured, machine-readable format.
questions.explain: Knowability of the steps is the deciding factor — since the invoice format and fields never change, the steps can be specified ahead of time, making this a workflow question regardless of how many calls or tools it uses. Needing more than one Claude call doesn't rule out a workflow, since workflows commonly chain several calls together. Needing external tools doesn't decide it either, since both workflows and agents can call tools. The output format is a separate design choice unrelated to whether the steps are knowable.

questions.q: A colleague describes a system that always executes the same three Claude calls in the same order for every request, because the task is fully understood ahead of time. What best describes what makes this a 'workflow' in the course's terms?
options: It only issues a single Claude call, structured internally into multiple process steps.
It runs a loop of Claude calls that terminates after a fixed number of iterations.
It is a predefined series of Claude calls built to solve a problem whose shape is already known.
It routes each request to one of several specialized pipelines chosen at runtime.
questions.explain: A workflow is a predefined series of Claude calls built for a problem whose shape is already known, which is exactly what makes it possible to design the three-call sequence in advance. Packing the same logic into a single call structured internally into steps isn't what makes something a workflow — it's the predefined, known series of calls. A loop terminating on a fixed iteration count describes a control structure, not the workflow/agent distinction itself. Routing a request to one of several pipelines chosen at runtime describes routing, a specific pattern within workflows, not workflows in general.

knowledgePoints.name: The trade, and the default
knowledgePoints.teach:
BenefitsDownsides
Workflowshigher accuracy (focus per subtask), easier to test and evaluate, more predictable, better for well-defined problemsless flexible, more constrained UX, more upfront design work
Agentsflexible UX, can combine tools in unexpected ways, handles novel situations, can ask for more inputlower success rate, harder to test and instrument, less predictable

Prefer workflows where possible. Only reach for agents when truly required.

The course's argument for the default is blunt: users want reliability, not a fancy agent. “Lower success rate” is not a footnote — it is the price of the flexibility, paid on every request including the ordinary ones.

questions.q: A product manager wants an agent for every new automation, since agents feel more powerful and flexible. Before approving the design, an architect pushes back citing the course's stated default. Which principle does she cite?
options: Default to agents everywhere since they can handle a strictly larger set of cases than workflows.
Choose whichever approach happens to be cheaper to operate at the team's current request volume.
Use agents for every user-facing request and workflows only for internal batch processing jobs.
Default to workflows and only reach for an agent when the steps genuinely cannot be predefined.
questions.explain: The course's stated default is workflows, reserved for agents only when the steps genuinely can't be predefined, because users want reliability more than flexibility. Claiming agents handle a strictly larger set of cases ignores that agents pay for that flexibility with a lower success rate. Picking based on operating cost sidesteps the actual tradeoff the course focuses on. Splitting by user-facing versus batch work isn't the distinction the course draws — it's about whether the steps are knowable, not who's waiting on the result.

questions.q: A team chooses workflows over agents for a new eligibility-checking feature. During planning, an engineer raises a concern about the tradeoff, expecting to spend meaningfully more time upfront. What downside are they anticipating?
options: Workflows require significantly more upfront design work and offer a more constrained user experience.
Workflows produce a measurably lower success rate for users than an equivalent agent would.
Workflows are considerably harder to test and evaluate end-to-end than an equivalent agent would be.
Workflows cannot invoke external tools at all as part of their execution steps, unlike agents.
questions.explain: More upfront design work and a more constrained user experience are the downsides the course attributes to workflows, since every step has to be predefined before the system can run. A lower success rate for users is actually the tradeoff on the agent side, not the workflow side. Workflows are described as easier to test and evaluate than agents, not harder, since each step can be checked individually. Workflows can and do invoke external tools as part of their steps, so that isn't a limitation unique to them.

reviewQuestions.q: An architect is justifying the extra risk of building an agent instead of a workflow for a research-assistant feature. Which of the following is the specific benefit unique to the agent approach that justifies the tradeoff?
options: It combines tools in sequences the designer never explicitly anticipated.
It reaches a higher accuracy on each individual subtask than a comparable workflow.
It is meaningfully easier to evaluate and test end-to-end than a workflow.
It produces more predictable behavior across repeated runs than a workflow.
reviewQuestions.explain: Combining tools in sequences nobody explicitly planned is the flexibility that's unique to agents, since a workflow's steps are all fixed in advance. Higher accuracy on each individual subtask is credited to workflows, precisely because each step can be a narrowly focused prompt. Being easier to evaluate and test is also a workflow strength, not an agent one, since an agent's path isn't known until it runs. More predictable behavior across runs likewise favors workflows, since agents are described as less predictable in exchange for their flexibility.

reviewQuestions.q: An observability engineer complains that they can't add per-stage latency metrics to a new agent the way they could for the workflow it replaced. What is the underlying reason?
options: Agent tool calls execute against a different network endpoint than workflow calls do.
Agents don't emit a stop_reason field the way workflow completions reliably do at each stage.
The agent's steps aren't fixed in advance, so there's no fixed stage to attach a metric to.
The agent's tool calls all run entirely server-side, outside the engineer's instrumentation.
reviewQuestions.explain: An agent's steps aren't fixed in advance, so there's no predetermined stage for a metric to attach to the way there is in a workflow. The network endpoint tool calls run against isn't what differs between agents and workflows. The presence or absence of a stop_reason field isn't the reason instrumentation is harder — the issue is that the sequence of steps doesn't exist until runtime. Where tool calls execute (client-side or server-side) is unrelated to why per-stage metrics are hard to define for an agent.

knowledgePoints.name: Fan out, then aggregate
knowledgePoints.teach:
Parallelization splits one complex task into multiple independent sub-tasks, runs them simultaneously, and aggregates the results into a final decision.

            ┌── credit check ────┐
loan app ───┼── fraud check ─────┼──→ aggregate ──→ decision
            └── affordability ───┘

The sub-tasks need not be identical — they are just meaningfully independent evaluations of the same thing.

Use it when a decision can be broken into independent evaluations. The aggregation step is part of the pattern, not an afterthought.

Two things it buys: latency, since the branches run at once, and accuracy, since each branch is a focused prompt rather than one prompt asked to weigh three concerns at the same time.

questions.q: A lending platform evaluates every loan application with a credit check, a fraud check, and an affordability check. These three checks don't depend on each other's results, and the team wants the fastest possible turnaround alongside a combined approval decision. Which orchestration pattern fits, and what must happen after the three checks finish?
options: Routing — classify the application, then send it to whichever single pipeline matches its risk profile.
Parallelization — run the three checks simultaneously, then aggregate the results into a decision.
Chaining — run the three checks one after another, each one revising the previous check's output.
Evaluator–optimizer — grade the application repeatedly against criteria until all three checks pass.
questions.explain: Independent evaluations that run at once and then combine into a single decision is the definition of parallelization, and aggregating the three results is the step that produces the final decision. Routing would send the application down only one of the three checks, not all three. Chaining would run the checks one after another with each revising the last, which isn't how independent checks like these relate to each other. Evaluator–optimizer implies a producer being graded and revised, not three independent checks being combined.

questions.q: A teammate objects to a parallelization design because the credit check, fraud check, and affordability check use different prompts and different criteria, arguing 'they're not the same task, so this can't be parallelization.' Is that objection correct?
options: Yes — parallelization requires applying the identical prompt to different inputs.
No — the branches only need to be genuinely independent, not identical to each other.
Yes, unless every one of the branches happens to be powered by the same underlying model.
No, but every branch must still return its output using exactly the same schema.
questions.explain: Parallelization only requires that the branches be genuinely independent evaluations — they don't need to be the identical prompt, since a credit check, a fraud check, and an affordability check are different tasks with different criteria. Requiring an identical prompt on different inputs describes something closer to a single prompt run repeatedly, not parallelization's actual requirement. The model powering each branch is a separate implementation choice unrelated to whether the branches count as parallelization. A shared output schema helps aggregation but isn't what defines the pattern.

reviewQuestions.q: A teammate asks why the fraud-check branch was split out into its own focused Claude call instead of just adding fraud rules to one big prompt that also does credit and affordability, given that running three calls at once already reduces total latency. What's the accuracy-related reason to keep them separate?
options: It lowers the total token cost incurred when running the three checks this way instead of as one.
It guarantees that the structured output format is honored correctly on every single run through.
It reduces the total number of round trips the overall workflow needs to make to the API.
Each branch stays a focused prompt, more accurate than one prompt juggling three concerns.
reviewQuestions.explain: Keeping each check as its own focused prompt tends to be more accurate than one prompt trying to weigh all three concerns simultaneously, since a focused prompt doesn't have to divide its attention. Running three calls doesn't inherently lower total token cost, since three focused prompts can easily add up to more tokens than one combined prompt. Structured output isn't guaranteed simply by splitting the checks apart. Running the checks as three parallel calls doesn't reduce round trips to the API — it takes three calls instead of one, just issued at the same time.

knowledgePoints.name: The long-prompt problem
knowledgePoints.teach:
Chaining breaks a large task into smaller sequential subtasks that build on each other.

It exists to solve one specific failure:

A single prompt with many constraints often gets some of them partially ignored.

Eight rules in one prompt reliably produces output obeying five. Not because any rule was unclear, but because attention is finite and they compete.

The two-step fix:

  1. Generate the content — imperfectly, that is expected.
  2. Revise in a focused pass targeting specific fixes only.

The second call is not the first call again. It carries the output and a short list of what to check, so nothing competes for attention.

questions.q: A single prompt asks Claude to rewrite a product description while following eight style rules — tone, length, banned words, required keywords, and so on. Testing shows the output reliably satisfies only five of the eight, even though none of the rules is ambiguous on its own. Which pattern addresses this, and how?
options: Parallelization — evaluate the description's compliance with each rule in a separate simultaneous call.
Chaining — generate the description first, then run a focused revision pass on just the missed rules.
Routing — classify the description by category and send it to a category-specific pipeline instead.
Evaluator–optimizer — grade the description and keep regenerating it from scratch until all eight pass.
questions.explain: Chaining is the fix for this exact failure: generate the description first, accepting that it will be imperfect, then run a second, focused revision pass that targets just the rules that were missed. Parallelization would check each rule independently but has no step that revises the draft to fix what it finds. Routing would send the description down one category-specific pipeline, which doesn't address a single description failing to satisfy all its own rules. Evaluator–optimizer implies grading against criteria and looping until accepted, which is a heavier mechanism than the two-step generate-then-revise fix this scenario calls for.

questions.q: In a two-step chain, the first call generates a draft that only partially satisfies the brief, which the course treats as expected rather than a failure. What is the second call's job, and what does it receive as input?
options: It re-runs the identical prompt again, but this time at a lower temperature setting.
It grades the first output against the criteria and returns only a numeric score.
It splits the first output into separate pieces for parallel processing downstream.
It takes the first output plus a short list of fixes and revises it in one focused pass.
questions.explain: The second call in a chain takes the first output plus a short, targeted list of what to fix, and revises it in a focused pass so nothing competes for the model's attention. Re-running the identical prompt at a lower temperature doesn't give the model any information about what specifically went wrong. Returning a numeric score describes an evaluator's job, not the second step of a two-step chain. Splitting the output into pieces for parallel processing describes parallelization, a different pattern entirely.

reviewQuestions.q: Two engineers are debating whether a multi-step content pipeline should be built as a chain or as a parallel fan-out. One points out that in their design, each step's output directly feeds the next step's input, and step three cannot start until step two finishes. What does that describe?
options: Chaining — the steps run one after another in sequence, each depending on the one before it.
Chaining — the steps use a single shared model, unlike parallelization's multiple models.
Chaining — the steps are for known work, while parallelization only handles unknown work.
Chaining — the final step aggregates results, which parallelization's final step never does.
reviewQuestions.explain: Chaining's steps run one after another, each depending on the output of the one before it, whereas parallelization's branches run at once with no such dependency. Chaining isn't distinguished by using a single shared model — both patterns can use whichever models fit each step. It also isn't about known versus unknown work — both patterns are workflow patterns built for known problems. And parallelization does have an aggregation step at the end, so aggregation isn't unique to chaining.

reviewQuestions.q: A prompt lists twelve formatting and content rules for a single Claude call. QA finds that several rules are dropped in most runs, even though each rule reads clearly on its own and the prompt is well under any length limit. What causes constraints to get dropped like this?
options: The constraints compete for a finite amount of the model's attention within one call.
The API silently truncates the prompt once it exceeds a certain number of rules.
Later instructions in the prompt overwrite the effect of the earlier ones entirely.
Any constraint listed after roughly the fifth position is effectively ignored by the model.
reviewQuestions.explain: Constraints get dropped because they compete for a finite amount of the model's attention within a single call, not because any one rule was unclear. The API doesn't truncate prompts based on how many rules they contain. Later instructions don't overwrite earlier ones outright — the failure is attention getting spread thin, not one rule silently replacing another. There's no fixed cutoff position after which rules stop being followed; which rules get dropped varies, because the mechanism is competition, not a hard limit.

knowledgePoints.name: Classify, then send down exactly one path
knowledgePoints.teach:
Routing categorises the input first — with a Claude call — then forwards it to one specialised pipeline built for that category.

                    ┌→ refund pipeline
inbox → classify ───┼→ bug-report pipeline
                    └→ sales pipeline

Input goes to exactly ONE pipeline. That is what lets each be deeply optimised for its own case.

Contrast with parallelization, where the input goes to all branches and the results are combined. Same fan shape on a diagram, opposite semantics.

The classification step is also where per-task model choice gets applied in practice: classify with Haiku, handle most categories with Sonnet, and let only the rare hard category reach Opus.

questions.q: A support inbox receives refund requests, bug reports, and sales enquiries, and the team wants each type handled by a pipeline built specifically for it. A classification call reads each incoming message first. Which pattern is this, and how many of the specialized pipelines does a single message reach?
options: Parallelization — the message is sent to all three pipelines, and their outputs are combined.
Chaining — the message passes through all three pipelines in sequence, one after another.
Routing — the message is classified and then sent to exactly one of the three pipelines.
Routing — the message is sent to one or more pipelines, depending on the classifier's confidence.
questions.explain: Routing is the pattern where a classification step reads the message and sends it to exactly one of the specialized pipelines, letting each pipeline be built for its specific case. Parallelization would send the message to all three pipelines and combine their outputs, which isn't what happens when only refund messages go to the refund pipeline. Chaining would pass the message through all three pipelines in sequence, which doesn't match a message being handled by only its own category's pipeline. Sending a message to more than one pipeline based on classifier confidence isn't how routing works — it always commits to a single branch.

questions.q: Sketched on a whiteboard, a routing design and a parallelization design both show one input branching into three boxes, which briefly confuses a new teammate into thinking they're the same pattern. What actually distinguishes them?
options: Routing runs its steps sequentially, while parallelization runs its branches all at once.
Routing always requires its output to be structured, while parallelization does not.
Routing relies on a single model tier, while parallelization uses several models at once.
Routing sends the input to exactly one branch, while parallelization sends it to all of them.
questions.explain: The real distinction is that routing sends the input to exactly one branch, while parallelization sends the same input to every branch and combines what comes back — the fan-out on a diagram looks the same, but the semantics are opposite. Routing isn't inherently more sequential than parallelization; a routed pipeline can still involve multiple sequential calls once it's chosen. Structured output isn't a requirement unique to routing. Neither pattern is defined by using one model tier versus several — model choice is a separate decision from which pattern is in play.

reviewQuestions.q: A team building a routing pipeline for support tickets is deciding which model tier should power the classification step that decides which of the three downstream pipelines a ticket goes to. What does the course recommend, and why?
options: The same tier as the downstream pipelines, so behavior stays consistent across the whole system.
Opus, since the team decides a misrouted ticket is too expensive to recover from later on.
A non-LLM classifier that the team trained offline before any of the pipelines were built.
A cheap tier such as Haiku, since classification is exactly the kind of narrow task it's suited for.
reviewQuestions.explain: Classification is exactly the kind of narrow, well-defined task a cheap tier like Haiku is suited for, and routing is where that kind of per-task model choice gets applied in practice. Matching the classification tier to the downstream pipelines' tier ignores that classification is a simpler task than actually handling the request. Reserving Opus for classification treats the cheapest step in the pipeline as if it were the hardest one. A non-LLM classifier trained offline is a different design entirely from the Claude-call classification step the course describes.

knowledgePoints.name: The loop that grades its own homework
knowledgePoints.teach:
Evaluator–optimizer: a producer creates output, a grader evaluates it against criteria, and if it is rejected the feedback loops back to the producer for revision. Repeat until accepted.

produce ──→ grade ──→ accepted? ──yes──→ done
   ↑                    │
   └────── feedback ────no

The course's example is an image-to-CAD workflow: describe the object, model it, render the model, grade the rendering against the original image, fix the issues, repeat.

It is the only one of the four patterns with a feedback edge back to its own first step.

The evaluator half is a model grader — and it inherits the model grader's rule: ask it for strengths, weaknesses and reasoning, not a bare number. Feedback that says “6/10” gives the producer nothing to act on.

questions.q: Of the four orchestration patterns covered — parallelization, chaining, routing, and evaluator–optimizer — only one has an edge in its diagram that loops output back to its own producing step when that output is rejected. Which pattern is this?
options: Parallelization, since a poor branch result triggers a rerun of just that one branch.
Evaluator–optimizer, since a rejected output loops feedback back to the producer for revision.
Chaining, since a failed revision pass restarts the entire chain from its first call.
Routing, since a misclassified input gets sent back to the classifier for a second pass.
questions.explain: Evaluator–optimizer is the only pattern where a rejected output loops feedback back to the producer for revision — the other three patterns all flow forward without looping back to an earlier step. Parallelization doesn't rerun a single branch based on quality; it runs all branches once and aggregates. Chaining's revision pass moves the work forward rather than restarting the whole chain from its first call. Routing doesn't send anything back to the classifier once a branch has been chosen.

questions.q: In an evaluator–optimizer loop, the grading call currently just returns a single number like '6/10' when it rejects an output, and the producer's revisions aren't improving much between iterations. What is the evaluator missing that the course says it needs to return?
options: A bare numeric score is enough, as long as acceptance is judged against a fixed threshold.
A complete rewritten version of the output for the producer to adopt directly.
Reasoning that names the output's specific strengths and weaknesses, not just a bare number.
A confidence interval expressing how certain the evaluator is in its own grade.
questions.explain: The evaluator has to return reasoning that names the output's specific strengths and weaknesses, since that's what gives the producer something concrete to act on when revising. A bare numeric score against a threshold tells the producer whether it passed but not what to change. Having the evaluator rewrite the output itself would collapse the separation between grading and producing that the pattern depends on. A confidence interval around the grade doesn't help the producer understand what was wrong with its output.

reviewQuestions.q: The course's image-to-CAD workflow describes an object, builds a CAD model from that description, and then renders the model before the evaluator step runs. What exactly does the evaluator compare in that final check?
options: It renders the model and compares that rendering against the original input image.
It compares the CAD model's geometry directly against a written specification document.
It compares the text description directly against the original input image itself.
It compares the final model against an earlier draft version of the same model.
reviewQuestions.explain: The check happens in the same medium as the input: the model gets rendered, and that rendering is compared against the original image. Comparing the CAD model's geometry to a written specification skips the rendering step the example actually describes. Comparing the text description to the original image checks the wrong stage — the description feeds the model, but it isn't what gets graded. Comparing the final model to an earlier draft would check progress between iterations, not fidelity to the original input.

knowledgePoints.name: The decision rule, and the four shapes
knowledgePoints.teach:
Given a scenario: if the steps are knowable in advance → design a workflow. If they are not, and the model must improvise across a flexible toolset → design an agent.

When the answer is workflow, pick by shape:

The scenario looks like…Pattern
independent evaluations to combine into one decisionParallelization
stages that build on each other; a prompt overloaded with rulesChaining
distinct categories, each needing different handlingRouting
quality that has to be iterated toward against criteriaEvaluator–optimizer

Two questions, in order. Which kind of thing, then which shape.

questions.q: Before picking among parallelization, chaining, routing, and evaluator–optimizer for a new automation, the course says there's a prior question to answer first — one that decides whether any of those four patterns even apply. What is that first question?
options: How many separate Claude calls will the finished design require?
Which model tier is appropriate for handling this particular task?
Does the task require access to any external tools at all?
Can the exact steps needed to solve this be pictured in advance?
questions.explain: The first question is whether the exact steps can be pictured in advance, since that's what decides between designing a workflow or an agent before any pattern-specific question comes up. How many Claude calls a design will need doesn't decide workflow versus agent, since both can involve multiple calls. Which model tier fits the task is a later decision made once the pattern is already chosen. Whether the task needs external tools doesn't distinguish them either, since both workflows and agents commonly use tools.

questions.q: A team is generating marketing copy that must be checked against a written style guide and revised repeatedly until it satisfies every criterion in that guide, however many passes that takes. Which of the four workflow patterns matches this shape?
options: Parallelization, since the style guide's criteria can be checked independently and combined.
Routing, since different copy types should be classified and sent to different pipelines.
Evaluator–optimizer, since output is graded against criteria and revised until it's accepted.
Chaining, since the copy is generated and then revised once in a focused second pass.
questions.explain: Grading output against explicit criteria and revising it until accepted is the evaluator–optimizer signature, which matches copy that must satisfy every rule in a style guide however many passes it takes. Parallelization would check independent aspects and combine them into one decision, not iterate a single piece of copy toward acceptance. Routing would classify the copy and send it to a different pipeline per type, not repeatedly revise the same piece. Chaining implies one focused revision pass, not an open-ended loop that continues until the criteria are met.

knowledgePoints.name: What you hand an agent
knowledgePoints.teach:
When the rule does land on agent, the design is not finished — it has just moved.

An agent is a goal plus a tool set. Claude figures out the combination of calls itself, including recognising when it needs more information from the user: asked to calculate a warranty expiry, it will ask for the purchase date rather than inventing one.

Design tools to be abstract and combinable, not hyper-specialised — the same principle, arrived at from the orchestration side.

Which closes the circle. The reason to prefer workflows is that agents have a lower success rate; the main lever you have on an agent's success rate is the quality and generality of its toolset.

questions.q: A team has concluded that a new customer-support automation can't have its steps predefined, so they're designing it as an agent rather than a workflow. According to the course, what does that design actually consist of handing the agent?
options: A fixed sequence of steps for it to execute, along with a set of tools to use.
A goal for it to accomplish, along with a set of tools to accomplish it with.
A goal to accomplish, along with a hard cap on how many iterations it may take.
A classified version of the input, along with the pipeline matching that classification.
questions.explain: An agent is handed a goal to accomplish along with a set of tools to accomplish it with, and it works out the combination of calls itself. Handing it a fixed sequence of steps plus tools would actually be building a workflow, since the steps would already be decided. Adding a hard cap on iterations describes an execution limit, not what defines the agent's design. Handing it a classified input and a matching pipeline describes routing, a workflow pattern, not an agent.

questions.q: A customer asks a support agent to check whether their product is still under warranty, but the purchase date isn't available anywhere in the conversation or the tools the agent has access to. What should the agent do, according to the course's description of expected agent behavior?
options: Fail immediately and return a clear error stating the request cannot be completed.
Assume the purchase date is today's date and proceed with the calculation anyway.
Ask the customer directly for the purchase date before proceeding any further.
Keep calling other available tools until one of them happens to supply a date.
questions.explain: Recognizing that it needs more information and asking the customer for the purchase date is the expected behavior the course describes, and it's presented as a benefit of the agent approach rather than a failure mode. Failing outright with an error would be unnecessarily rigid when the missing information could simply be asked for. Assuming today's date and proceeding would silently produce a wrong answer instead of surfacing the missing input. Calling other tools hoping one supplies a date isn't a substitute for asking the customer directly, since none of the agent's tools would actually have that information.

reviewQuestions.q: An operations team receives incoming documents that fall into exactly three types — contracts, invoices, and correspondence — and each type needs a completely different specialized prompt to process correctly. Which orchestration pattern matches this description?
options: Routing — classify each document, then send it to the one pipeline built for its type.
Parallelization — run all three specialized prompts on every document and combine the results.
Chaining — run the three specialized prompts in sequence on every incoming document.
An agent — give the model all three prompts as tools and let it choose one per document.
reviewQuestions.explain: Distinct document categories that each need different handling, with a classification step choosing one pipeline per document, is exactly the routing shape. Running all three specialized prompts on every document and combining the results describes parallelization, not triage into distinct types. Running the three prompts in sequence on every document describes chaining, which doesn't fit documents that only need one type of handling each. Framing the three prompts as tools for an agent to pick from turns a known, enumerable choice into an open-ended one, when the categories are already fixed.

reviewQuestions.q: A team is scoping a research tool that must handle arbitrary user questions, combining a search tool, a calculator, and a document reader in whatever order turns out to be needed — a combination the team readily admits they can't enumerate in advance. Should this be built as a workflow or an agent?
options: A workflow, covering only the common cases the team can currently predict.
An agent, since the necessary steps genuinely cannot be known ahead of time.
A workflow using routing, with a catch-all 'other' branch for edge cases.
Either approach works equally well; the choice is just a matter of style preference.
reviewQuestions.explain: Requests whose combination of steps genuinely can't be enumerated ahead of time is the rule's second branch stated almost exactly — that's what should push the design toward an agent rather than a workflow. Limiting the workflow to only the common, predictable cases would leave the genuinely novel requests unhandled, which is the situation being described. Adding a routing branch for 'other' still requires the steps within that branch to be knowable, which the scenario says they aren't. Treating the choice as a matter of style ignores that the course ties the decision to a specific, checkable fact about whether the steps can be predicted.
